direct_answer:
Aker BP states that it conducted a double materiality assessment (DMA) using a systematic, four-step process to identify material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) and the associated sustainability matters, covering both (i) impact materiality (inside-out: impacts on environment and society) and (ii) financial materiality (outside-in: financial risks and opportunities to the business model and performance, including reputational risk and dependencies on natural, human and social resources) [Source 1][Source 5]. The assessment mapped IROs, their dependencies, and their connection to Aker BP’s own operations and value chain, considering activities, business relationships and geographies; it focused on oil and gas production for own operations, development projects for the upstream value chain, and also noted downstream impacts from the use of petroleum products [Source 3][Source 5].

Stakeholder engagement is described as an input to the DMA: Aker BP maintains dialogue with stakeholders to identify risks, opportunities and actual/potential impacts, including public consultations for PDO impact assessments (shared with “over 40 key stakeholders”), publication of impact assessments, and a whistleblowing channel [Source 2]. For the 2024 DMA, Aker BP incorporated stakeholder perspectives via in-depth interviews and workshops with internal management and subject matter experts, and notes that the 2024 process was based on prior-year interviews involving owners, key suppliers, customers, NGOs and authorities [Source 2].

For prioritisation, Aker BP explains that IRO assessments use a severity × likelihood approach (similar to consequence × probability in enterprise risk management), using company scales and the shared company risk matrix; IROs are documented in the same tool as other risks and prioritised/handled together [Source 1]. It also states that it pays “special attention” to dependencies between impacts and related risks/opportunities, and that outcomes were reviewed by the Board of Directors (BoD), Audit and Risk Committee (ARC) and Executive Management Team (EMT) [Source 1][Source 6].

Sustainability matters identified as material from both an impact and a financial perspective (i.e., high impact and high financial relevance/strategic priority) are: climate change, own workforce, pollution, business conduct, and resource use and circular economy [Source 3].
compliance_rationale: The report provides a clear description that the DMA covers both impact and financial materiality, includes value chain considerations, uses a severity×likelihood rating aligned with enterprise risk management, and incorporates stakeholder perspectives, with governance validation by BoD/ARC/EMT [Source 1][Source 2][Source 3][Source 5][Source 6]. However, the retrieved passages do not evidence the specific qualitative/quantitative thresholds used to determine materiality, nor do they fully evidence how impact-materiality criteria (scale/scope/irremediable character) and financial-materiality magnitude criteria were applied, beyond stating severity×likelihood and use of company scales [Source 1].
disclosure_gaps: Specific qualitative and/or quantitative thresholds (cut-offs) used to determine which IROs/topics are material are not provided in the retrieved passages [Source 1].
Detailed application of impact materiality criteria (e.g., explicit assessment of scale, scope and irremediable character for negative impacts) is not evidenced in the retrieved passages [Source 1].

Detailed application of financial materiality criteria (e.g., magnitude of potential financial effects on financial position/performance/cash flows/access to finance/cost of capital) is not evidenced in the retrieved passages; the report notes challenges in measuring financial effects but does not provide the criteria/thresholds used [Source 6].

Explicit description of interdependencies leading to cases where financial materiality is identified without related impacts (or vice versa) is not evidenced beyond a general statement of paying special attention to dependencies [Source 1].
Explicit disclosure of cross-matter effects/trade-offs (actions on one matter creating material negative impacts/risks on another) is not evidenced in the retrieved passages.
key_findings: DMA covers both impact (inside-out) and financial (outside-in) materiality, including reputational risk and dependencies on natural, human and social resources [Source 1].

Assessment maps IROs and their dependencies across own operations and upstream/downstream value chain; considers activities, business relationships and geographies; focuses own-operations assessment on oil and gas production and upstream value chain on development projects [Source 3][Source 5].

Stakeholder engagement informs the DMA through multiple channels (PDO impact assessment consultations, publication of impact assessments, whistleblowing channel) and through interviews/workshops; key stakeholders cited include owners, suppliers, customers, NGOs and authorities [Source 2].
IROs are assessed and prioritised using severity×likelihood, aligned with enterprise risk management tools and scales, and reviewed by BoD/ARC/EMT [Source 1][Source 6].
Sustainability matters identified as material from both impact and financial perspectives: climate change, own workforce, pollution, business conduct, resource use and circular economy [Source 3].
